stem.text: Humans detect the sweet taste of sucrose sugar using chemoreceptor cells in taste buds on the tongue. The red admiral butterfly, Vanessa atalanta, detects sucrose using chemoreceptor cells located on its antennae and on its tarsi (feet). The mode of action of the chemoreceptors in V. atalanta is similar to that in humans.
Fig. 10.1 shows the locations of the chemoreceptor cells on V. atalanta.

stem.alt: Photograph of a red admiral butterfly with its wings open, with lines labelling its antennae at the top of its head and its tarsi (feet) at the tips of its legs resting on a ledge.

stem.text: Describe how the presence of sucrose causes an action potential in the sensory neurone associated with a chemoreceptor cell in V. atalanta.

points.text: sucrose binds to, receptor protein / (chemoreceptor) cell surface receptor ;
(named) neurotransmitter vesicles, move towards / fuse with, (presynaptic) membrane ;
(named) neurotransmitter binds to receptor on, sensory neurone / postsynaptic membrane ;

explanation.text: Sucrose binds to a receptor protein on the chemoreceptor cell's surface, which triggers an intracellular second messenger. This leads to Na+ entering the chemoreceptor cell, depolarising its membrane and creating a receptor (generator) potential; if this is big enough, Ca2+ ions then enter the cell, causing neurotransmitter-containing vesicles to move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptors on the sensory neurone's postsynaptic membrane, opening ligand-gated Na+ channels there, so Na+ enters the sensory neurone and depolarises it; if this depolarisation reaches threshold, an action potential is triggered in the sensory neurone.

reasoningChain: Sucrose binds a receptor protein on the chemoreceptor cell, triggering a second messenger.
This causes Na+ entry and depolarisation, generating a receptor (generator) potential in the chemoreceptor cell.
Ca2+ enters the chemoreceptor cell, causing neurotransmitter vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.
Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the sensory neurone, opening Na+ channels there and depolarising it.
If depolarisation of the sensory neurone reaches threshold, an action potential is generated.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the chemoreceptor cell's own depolarisation as if it were directly an action potential in the sensory neurone, skipping the synaptic transmission step between the two cells.
